# Closing the loop: Ashby's ultrastable system and why today's AI systems disappoint

*An Ultrastable white paper. Ultrastable is the foundation for any autonomous system.*

## Executive summary

Many people believe that AI systems are smart enough already; what holds them back is model capability. This paper argues otherwise: what holds most AI systems back is an open loop: nothing checks the result against limits and changes the system when it fails. That is an engineering property, and it can be tested.

Ultrastable takes its name from Ashby's ultrastable system. Most current AI systems answer and stop: nothing checks the result against limits and changes the system when it fails, so their loops stay open. We state Ashby's mechanism as a set of testable properties, check each against this system's code and records, and show where the code falls short.

It is written for people who build or run AI systems and want them to keep working without someone watching. It names 5 concrete problems, the mechanism that answers each one, and how to put that mechanism in place.

## 1. The problem

An adaptive system keeps its essential variables within limits through two feedbacks: a first loop that reacts to the environment, and a second loop that changes the first loop's parameters (step-functions) only when an essential variable leaves its limits, and keeps changing them until a configuration holds the variables in bounds. [1]

This matters now because the usual answer, AI is held back by model capability, sends teams after the wrong fix. A better model or another reviewer does not close a loop that nothing checks.

The problems in detail:

1. An essential variable without limits. In Ashby's account, adaptation is defined by keeping certain essential variables within limits. A variable with no limits can never trigger the second loop, so a system that declares one without limits is not ultrastable in that variable. [1]
2. A second loop that never acts. The second feedback runs through the essential variables: when one leaves its limits, the system changes itself. A second loop that is declared but never steps is a diagram, not a mechanism. [1]
3. Nothing the second loop can change. Ashby's preface: "any system which shows adaptation must (1) contain many variables that behave as step-functions". The second loop changes the first loop's parameters; where it can only file a work item, the change waits on another loop. [1]
4. A search that stops before anything holds. The ultrastable system keeps changing its step-functions until it reaches a configuration that holds the essential variables within limits, and then keeps it. A loop that gives up after a fixed list of tries, or never finds a configuration that holds, has not adapted. [1]
5. AI systems leave their loops open. Ultrastable's reading, not Ashby's words: a chat model or coding agent produces an answer and stops. Nothing checks the result against limits and changes the system when it fails, so the loop is open, and disappointment follows. Every loop Ultrastable runs is meant to carry its own closing check. [1]

## 2. The approach

The approach follows Ashby's ultrastable system [1]: a first loop acts on the world, and a second loop changes the first loop's settings whenever a variable that matters leaves its limits, and keeps changing them until it is back inside.

Ultrastable is that design as working code [2]. For each problem above it uses a specific mechanism:

1. An essential variable without limits: every essential variable is declared with its limits, per scope (platform, tenant) (ULTRASTABILITY-1, `doctrine/ultrastability.json`); the check fails when an essential variable has neither a lower nor an upper limit (ASHBY-1, `foundation/ultrastability.py`)
2. A second loop that never acts: after patience_ticks readings out of limits, one step is taken and logged with a prediction (ULTRASTABILITY-1, `foundation/ultrastability.py`); the second loop runs on the watchdog clock and on the cost guard, server-side (CLOCKWORK-1, `.github/workflows/watchdog.yml`)
3. Nothing the second loop can change: a ladder step of kind param changes a declared value the first loop reads, inside declared limits (ULTRASTABILITY-1, `doctrine/ultrastability.json`)
4. A search that stops before anything holds: after the ladder, untried parameter values are drawn until one holds or the declared range is spent; only then a redesign item (ASHBY-SEARCH-1, `foundation/ultrastability.py`); a step is kept only when the variable is back inside its limits within settle_ticks; otherwise it is undone (ULTRASTABILITY-1, `foundation/ultrastability.py`)
5. AI systems leave their loops open: an output with no code consumer fails the build (CLOSED-LOOP-1, `foundation/closedloop.py`); every loop has a server-side owner; a client session never closes one (SERVER-OWNS-LOOPS-1, `foundation/loopowner.py`)

## 3. Putting it into practice

To apply this to your own system, one step per problem:

1. An essential variable without limits. Put in place: every essential variable is declared with its limits, per scope (platform, tenant). Check it with one number, share of declared essential variables that have limits (doctrine/ultrastability.json), and set a limit for it (>= 1.0 is the limit we use).
2. A second loop that never acts. Put in place: after patience_ticks readings out of limits, one step is taken and logged with a prediction. Check it with one number, second-order steps the ultrastability loop took in the last 30 days (ops/ultrastability.jsonl), and set a limit for it (>= 1 is the limit we use).
3. Nothing the second loop can change. Put in place: a ladder step of kind param changes a declared value the first loop reads, inside declared limits. Check it with one number, share of essential variables whose second loop can change a parameter of the first loop, and set a limit for it (>= 0.5 is the limit we use).
4. A search that stops before anything holds. Put in place: after the ladder, untried parameter values are drawn until one holds or the declared range is spent; only then a redesign item. Check it with one number, share of second-order steps that brought the variable back inside its limits and were kept, and set a limit for it (>= 0.25 is the limit we use).
5. AI systems leave their loops open. Put in place: an output with no code consumer fails the build. Check it with one number, share of registered loops that declare a closing probe and a server-side owner, and set a limit for it (>= 1.0 is the limit we use).

In our own system, 4 of 5 of these checks pass today. Share of declared essential variables that have limits (doctrine/ultrastability.json) reads 1.0 (n = 19; source: doctrine/ultrastability.json). Second-order steps the ultrastability loop took in the last 30 days (ops/ultrastability.jsonl) reads 172 (n = 23323; source: ops/ultrastability.jsonl). Share of essential variables whose second loop can change a parameter of the first loop reads 0.737 (n = 19; source: doctrine/ultrastability.json). Where a check fails, a work item carries the fix, and it closes only when the same check passes.

## 4. Trade-offs and limits

- Reading. Chapters 7 and 8 were not machine-read for this paper: the archive.org text the research loop could reach ends in chapter 2. Ashby's mechanism is stated here in our own words from the book's contents and preface; the only verbatim quotation is from the preface (page v).
- Search. Ashby's step-functions take new values at random. Ultrastable first takes a fixed ladder of steps, then draws untried values at random (seeded, so a run can be replayed) from each parameter's declared range. A restructure step is a work item for the executor, not a step-function, and depends on the executor completing it.
- Declared versus observed. The closed-loop share counts loops that declare a closing probe and a server-side owner; it does not show that each probe passes today.
- Source. Book, version 1952, reprinted with corrections 1954.
